title: Dido supplex. Responsum Aeneae
titleEn: Dido's Plea and Aeneas's Answer — Aeneid IV.305–407
about: Dido confronts Aeneas. Did he really hope to hide so great a wrong and slip away from her land in silence? Does nothing hold him: not their love, not the hand once pledged, not the cruel death she will die? He is even fitting out his fleet in the winter storms, when he would not sail like this to Troy itself if Troy still stood. By her tears and by his own right hand, by their marriage, if she has ever deserved anything of him, she begs him to pity a falling house and give up his purpose. Because of him the African tribes and her own Tyrians hate her, and her honour and the good name that raised her to the stars are gone. What is she waiting for: for her brother Pygmalion to raze her walls, or for Iarbas to carry her off? If only she had a little Aeneas playing in her hall, whose face would bring his father back, she would not feel so wholly abandoned. Aeneas, held by Jupiter's warning, keeps his eyes fixed and forces down his pain. He will never deny what she deserves of him, he says, nor regret remembering Elissa while he lives. But he never meant to steal away, and he never offered marriage. If the fates let him live as he chose, he would be rebuilding Troy; now Apollo's oracles order him to Italy, and that is his love and his country. She has her Carthage; why grudge the Trojans a land of their own? His father's ghost troubles his sleep, and he is cheating his son of his kingdom; and now Mercury himself, sent by Jupiter, has brought the command, and Aeneas saw and heard him with his own senses. He goes to Italy not of his own will. Dido, who has been watching him all the while with silent, roaming eyes, bursts out: no goddess bore him, but the Caucasus, and tigers nursed him. Did he weep or look at her or pity her? She rescued him shipwrecked and destitute and shared her kingdom with him; now it is Apollo and oracles and messengers of the gods. Let him go and seek Italy over the waves: she hopes he will drink his punishment among the rocks and call on Dido's name, and she will follow him with black fires, and haunt him as a ghost when she is dead. She breaks off and is carried fainting to her marble chamber by her maids. Aeneas, though he longs to comfort her and groans under the weight of his love, obeys the gods and returns to the fleet. The Trojans launch the tarred ships and bring leafy oars and unshaped timber from the woods, streaming out of the city like ants carrying off a heap of grain against the winter, a black column busy along a narrow track.

sentences.t:
“Dissimulare etiam sperasti, perfide, tantum
posse nefas, tacitusque mea decedere terra?
sentences.l:
“To conceal even did you hope, faithless one, so great
a wrong to be able, and silent from my land to depart?
sentences.i: “Did you hope, faithless man, that you could even hide so great a wrong, and leave my land without a word?
sentences.n: Dido's speech opens here, so Greenough prints the opening quotation mark; it runs to line 330. This line begins a new paragraph in Greenough. 'sperasti' is a shortened (syncopated) form of 'speravisti', perfect of 'spero'. 'Dissimulare' depends on 'posse', and 'posse' on 'sperasti': 'did you hope to be able to conceal'. 'perfide' is a vocative. 'tantum… nefas' is split across the line-end, with 'posse' between; 'nefas' is an indeclinable neuter noun, 'an impious act'. 'tacitus' is an adjective where English would use an adverb, 'silently'. 'decedere' also depends on 'posse'; 'mea… terra' is an ablative of separation, 'from my land'.

sentences.t:
Nec te noster amor, nec te data dextera quondam,
nec moritura tenet crudeli funere Dido?
sentences.l:
Does not you our love, nor you the right hand given once,
nor Dido about to die by a cruel death hold?
sentences.i: Does nothing hold you back: not our love, not the hand you once gave me, not Dido, who will die a cruel death?
sentences.n: Three subjects ('amor', 'dextera', 'Dido') share one singular verb, 'tenet', which stands in the last line, after 'moritura'; 'te' is repeated for emphasis (anaphora with 'nec… nec… nec'). 'data' is the perfect passive participle of 'do', agreeing with 'dextera': the right hand given as a pledge. 'moritura' is the future participle of 'morior', 'about to die', agreeing with 'Dido'; 'crudeli funere' is an ablative, 'by a cruel death'. Dido names herself in the third person.

sentences.t:
Quin etiam hiberno moliris sidere classem,
et mediis properas aquilonibus ire per altum,
crudelis?
sentences.l:
Why, even under a wintry star you are working at your fleet,
and in the midst of the north winds you hurry to go over the deep,
cruel one?
sentences.i: What, are you even fitting out your fleet under a winter sky, and hurrying to put to sea with the north winds at their height, cruel man?
sentences.n: 'Quin etiam' is 'why, even': it adds a worse charge. 'hiberno… sidere' is an ablative of time, 'under a wintry star', i.e. in the stormy season when no one sails. 'moliris' is the second person singular present of the deponent 'molior', 'labour at, set in motion'. 'mediis… aquilonibus' is an ablative of attendant circumstance, 'with the north winds at their height'. 'altum' is a neuter adjective used as a noun, 'the deep (sea)'. 'crudelis' is a vocative; adjectives of the third declension have a vocative the same as the nominative. The word is held over to the next line for weight.

sentences.t:
Quid, si non arva aliena domosque
ignotas peteres, sed Troia antiqua maneret,
Troia per undosum peteretur classibus aequor
Mene fugis?
sentences.l:
What, if not fields foreign and homes
unknown you were seeking, but Troy ancient were still standing,
would Troy be sought by fleets across the wave-filled sea?
Is it me you flee?
sentences.i: Tell me: if it were not foreign fields and unknown homes you were seeking, but ancient Troy still stood, would even Troy be sought with a fleet across the stormy sea? Is it from me you are running?
sentences.n: A conditional contrary to fact in present time: 'peteres' and 'maneret' are imperfect subjunctives in the 'si' clause, and 'peteretur' is the imperfect subjunctive of the conclusion. The point: he would not sail in winter even for Troy, so it must be Dido he is escaping. 'arva aliena domosque ignotas' — 'domos' ends one line and 'ignotas' begins the next. 'Troia' is repeated (anaphora). 'undosum' is 'full of waves'. Greenough prints no punctuation between 'aequor' and 'Mene', so the unit runs on to the question mark. 'Mene' is 'me' with the question particle '-ne'; 'me' is the object of 'fugis', put first for emphasis.

sentences.t:
Per ego has lacrimas dextramque tuam te
(quando aliud mihi iam miserae nihil ipsa reliqui)
per conubia nostra, per inceptos hymenaeos,
si bene quid de te merui, fuit aut tibi quicquam
dulce meum, miserere domus labentis, et istam—
sentences.l:
By, I, these tears and your right hand, you
(since nothing else to myself, wretched, now I myself have left)
by our marriage, by the wedding-songs begun,
if well anything of you I have deserved, or there was to you anything
sweet of mine, pity a house falling, and that —
sentences.i: By these tears, and by your own right hand, I beg you (since I have left myself, poor wretch, nothing else to plead by), by our marriage, by the wedding rites we had begun, if I have ever deserved any kindness of you, or anything of mine was ever sweet to you, take pity on a falling house, and that —
sentences.n: The great appeal. 'Per… te' with 'oro' in the next line is the formula of entreaty: 'per' with the accusative, 'by', names what the speaker appeals to, and 'ego' is tucked in between 'per' and its noun 'lacrimas', a regular Latin order in entreaties; 'te' is the object of 'oro'. 'quando' is causal, 'since'. 'mihi… miserae' is a dative ('for wretched me'); 'ipsa' is nominative, 'I myself'; 'reliqui' is the perfect of 'relinquo'. 'conubia' is a neuter plural; 'hymenaeos' is a Greek noun, accusative plural, 'wedding songs', i.e. the wedding; 'inceptos', 'begun', because to her it was a marriage. 'quid' after 'si' is indefinite ('anything'). 'aut' stands second in its clause. 'quicquam… meum' is 'anything of mine', with 'dulce' as predicate: 'if anything of mine was sweet to you'. 'miserere' is the imperative of the deponent 'misereor', which takes the genitive ('domus labentis'). 'istam' breaks off with a dash at the line's end: its noun 'mentem' comes only after the parenthesis in the next line.

sentences.t: oro, si quis adhuc precibus locus—exue mentem.
sentences.l: I beg, if any still for prayers place — put off purpose.
sentences.i: I beg you, if there is any room left for prayers — strip off that purpose of yours.
sentences.n: 'oro' governs the 'te' of line 314. 'si quis adhuc precibus locus' is a parenthesis with 'est' understood; 'quis' is the indefinite 'any' after 'si', and 'precibus' is a dative, 'for prayers'. 'exue' is the imperative of 'exuo', 'take off' (of clothing): she asks him to put off his resolve like a garment. 'istam… mentem' (line 318) is split by the whole parenthesis, so the sentence closes on its object.

sentences.t:
Te propter Libycae gentes Nomadumque tyranni
odere, infensi Tyrii;
sentences.l:
You because of, the Libyan nations and the Nomads' tyrants
hate me, hostile are the Tyrians;
sentences.i: Because of you the Libyan tribes and the Numidian chiefs hate me, and my own Tyrians are hostile;
sentences.n: 'Te propter' puts the preposition after its object (anastrophe); it is repeated at once. 'Nomadum' is the genitive plural of 'Nomades', the nomads of Numidia. 'odere' = 'oderunt', the perfect of 'odi', which has present meaning: 'they hate'. You have seen this '-ere' ending constantly. With 'infensi Tyrii', supply 'sunt'. 'me' is understood with 'odere'.

sentences.t:
te propter eundem
exstinctus pudor, et, qua sola sidera adibam,
fama prior.
sentences.l:
you because of, the same,
extinguished is my honour, and, by which alone to the stars I was going,
my former fame.
sentences.i: because of you, the same man, my honour has been put out, and the good name I once had, by which alone I was rising to the stars.
sentences.n: 'eundem' agrees with 'te': 'you, the very same'. With 'exstinctus' supply 'est'. 'pudor' is a woman's honour, here Dido's vow of faithfulness to her dead husband Sychaeus. 'qua sola' is an ablative, 'by which alone', and refers forward to 'fama'. 'sidera adibam' is the imperfect, 'I was on my way to the stars', i.e. to lasting renown. 'fama prior' is held back to the next line as the climax.

sentences.t: Cui me moribundam deseris, hospes?
sentences.l: To whom me, dying, do you abandon, guest?
sentences.i: To whom are you leaving me, to die, my guest?
sentences.n: 'Cui' is a dative, 'to whom'. 'moribundam' agrees with 'me', 'at the point of death'. 'deseris' is the present. 'hospes' is a vocative: the word means both 'guest' and 'host', and it is the bond of hospitality that Dido falls back on, as the next line explains.

sentences.t: Hoc solum nomen quoniam de coniuge restat.
sentences.l: This alone name since from 'husband' remains.
sentences.i: Since that is the only name now left of a husband.
sentences.n: 'quoniam' is put after the words it introduces. 'de coniuge' is 'out of (the name of) husband': 'hospes' is all that is left of 'coniunx'. 'restat' is 'remains'. The line explains the bitterness of the vocative 'hospes' before it.

sentences.t: Quid moror?
sentences.l: Why do I delay?
sentences.i: What am I waiting for?
sentences.n: 'Quid' is 'why'. 'moror' is the present of the deponent 'moror', 'delay'.

sentences.t:
An mea Pygmalion dum moenia frater
destruat, aut captam ducat Gaetulus Iarbas?
sentences.l:
Or my, Pygmalion, until walls, my brother,
destroy, or me captured lead away Gaetulian Iarbas?
sentences.i: For my brother Pygmalion to tear down my walls, or for Iarbas the Gaetulian to carry me off as his captive?
sentences.n: 'An' introduces a further question, ironically answering the one before. 'dum' with the subjunctive ('destruat', 'ducat') is 'until'. Pygmalion, Dido's brother, murdered her husband Sychaeus (Book I); she fled Tyre with his treasure. 'mea… moenia' and 'Pygmalion… frater' are interlaced. 'captam' agrees with an understood 'me'. 'ducat' can mean both 'lead off as a captive' and 'take as a wife': Iarbas is the suitor she refused. 'Gaetulus' is 'Gaetulian', of a people of north Africa.

sentences.t:
Saltem si qua mihi de te suscepta fuisset
ante fugam suboles, si quis mihi parvulus aula
luderet Aeneas, qui te tamen ore referret,
non equidem omnino capta ac deserta viderer.”
sentences.l:
At least if any to me from you received had been
before your flight offspring, if some to me tiny in the hall
were playing Aeneas, who you nevertheless in face would bring back,
not indeed altogether captured and deserted would I seem.”
sentences.i: At least, if I had had a child by you before you fled, if some little Aeneas were playing in my hall, who in spite of all would bring you back to me in his face, I would not seem so wholly a captive and abandoned.”
sentences.n: 'si qua' and 'si quis' have the indefinite 'qua'/'quis', 'any', 'some'. 'suscepta fuisset' is a pluperfect subjunctive passive (with 'fuisset' for 'esset'), 'had been received': 'suscipere' is used of having a child (literally of taking up a newborn as one's own). 'suboles' is 'offspring', held back to the next line. 'parvulus' is a diminutive, 'tiny'. 'aula' is an ablative of place. 'luderet' and 'viderer' are imperfect subjunctives in a conditional contrary to fact. 'qui… referret' is a relative clause with the subjunctive; 'tamen', 'in spite of all', and 'ore', an ablative, 'in his face'. 'viderer' is passive of 'video', 'seem'. 'capta' picks up 'captam' (326). The closing quotation mark is Greenough's: Dido's speech ends here.

sentences.t: Dixerat.
sentences.l: She had spoken.
sentences.i: She had spoken.
sentences.n: 'Dixerat' is the pluperfect: a regular way to close a speech in Virgil. This line begins a new paragraph in Greenough.

sentences.t:
Ille Iovis monitis immota tenebat
lumina, et obnixus curam sub corde premebat.
sentences.l:
He by Jove's warnings unmoved kept
his eyes, and, straining, his care under his heart pressed down.
sentences.i: He, because of Jupiter's warning, kept his eyes unmoved, and with a struggle pressed down the pain beneath his heart.
sentences.n: 'Iovis monitis' is an ablative of cause, 'because of Jupiter's warnings' (Mercury's message in the last part). 'immota' is predicative, agreeing with 'lumina' ('eyes'): 'kept his eyes unmoved'. 'obnixus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'obnitor', 'strain against', with present sense. 'curam' is 'care', the anxiety of love. 'premebat' is the imperfect.

sentences.t: Tandem pauca refert:
sentences.l: At last a few things he returns:
sentences.i: At last he answered briefly:
sentences.n: 'pauca' is a neuter plural, 'a few words'. 'refert' is a historic present, 'replies'.

sentences.i: “I shall never deny, my queen, that you have deserved of me all the many kindnesses you can count over in words;
sentences.n: Aeneas's speech opens here, so Greenough prints the opening quotation mark (mid-line); it runs to line 361. 'te… promeritam' is an accusative and infinitive with 'esse' understood, after 'negabo': 'I will deny that you have deserved'. 'promeritam' is the perfect participle of 'promereor', 'deserve', and its object is the 'quae plurima' clause: '(the things) which, very many as they are, you can list'. 'quae' is neuter plural (the services), not 'who'. 'fando' is the ablative of the gerund of 'fari', 'speak': 'by speaking'. 'regina' is a vocative: he addresses her by her title.

sentences.t:
nec me meminisse pigebit Elissae,
dum memor ipse mei, dum spiritus hos regit artus.
sentences.l:
nor me to remember will it irk of Elissa,
while mindful myself of me, while breath these limbs rules.
sentences.i: nor will I ever be sorry to remember Elissa, so long as I remember myself, so long as breath governs these limbs.
sentences.n: 'pigebit' is the future of the impersonal 'piget', 'it irks', which takes the accusative of the person ('me') and an infinitive ('meminisse'). 'meminisse' is a perfect in form with present meaning, and takes the genitive ('Elissae'). Elissa is Dido's other name. With 'dum memor ipse mei' supply 'sum'; 'mei' is the genitive of 'ego' with 'memor'. 'hos… artus' is 'these limbs'. Notice the double 'dum'.

sentences.t: Pro re pauca loquar.
sentences.l: For the matter few things I shall speak.
sentences.i: I will say a few words to the point.
sentences.n: 'Pro re' is 'for the case', 'as the matter requires'. 'loquar' is the future of the deponent 'loquor' (the form is the same as the present subjunctive).

sentences.t:
Neque ego hanc abscondere furto
speravi—ne finge—fugam, nec coniugis umquam
praetendi taedas, aut haec in foedera veni.
sentences.l:
Neither I this to hide by stealth
hoped — do not pretend — flight, nor of a husband ever
held out the torches, or into these compacts came.
sentences.i: I never hoped to hide this departure by stealth (do not imagine it), nor did I ever hold out the torches of a husband, or enter into any such compact.
sentences.n: 'hanc… fugam' is a hyperbaton across the line and a parenthesis. 'furto' is an ablative of manner, 'by stealth'. 'ne finge' is a poetic prohibition, 'ne' with the imperative ('don't make that up'); Greenough prints it between dashes without spaces, so it stays inside the unit. 'coniugis… taedas' are the wedding torches of a husband: carrying torches was part of a Roman wedding procession. 'praetendi' is the perfect, 'held out before me'. 'haec in foedera' is 'into this kind of treaty', i.e. a marriage bond.

sentences.t:
Me si fata meis paterentur ducere vitam
auspiciis et sponte mea componere curas,
urbem Troianam primum dulcisque meorum
reliquias colerem, Priami tecta alta manerent,
et recidiva manu posuissem Pergama victis.
sentences.l:
Me, if the fates allowed by my own to lead my life
auspices and by my own will to settle my cares,
the city Trojan first and the sweet of my own people
remains I would tend, Priam's lofty roofs would remain,
and, reborn, by my hand I would have set up Pergamum for the conquered.
sentences.i: If the fates allowed me to live my life by my own guidance and settle my troubles as I wished, I would be caring first for the city of Troy and the dear remains of my people, Priam's high palace would still stand, and with my own hand I would have raised a reborn citadel for the defeated.
sentences.n: A conditional contrary to fact: 'paterentur' (imperfect subjunctive) in the 'si' clause; 'colerem' and 'manerent' (imperfect subjunctive) for present time, and 'posuissem', the pluperfect subjunctive, for what would already have been done. 'Me' is put first, object of 'paterentur' and subject of 'ducere'. 'meis… auspiciis' is a Roman military phrase: a general fought 'under his own auspices', on his own authority. 'sponte mea' is an ablative, 'of my own accord'. 'dulcis' = 'dulces', the '-is' accusative plural Greenough prints, agreeing with 'reliquias'. 'Pergama' is a neuter plural, the citadel of Troy; 'recidiva' agrees with it, 'rising again'. 'victis' is a dative, 'for the conquered'.

sentences.t:
Sed nunc Italiam magnam Gryneus Apollo,
Italiam Lyciae iussere capessere sortes:
sentences.l:
But now Italy, great, Grynean Apollo,
Italy the Lycian lots have ordered to seize:
sentences.i: But now it is to great Italy that Grynean Apollo, to Italy that the Lycian oracles, have commanded me to make my way:
sentences.n: 'Italiam' is repeated at the start of the phrase (anaphora): it is the object of 'capessere', 'make for, take hold of'. Apollo is 'Gryneus' from his shrine at Grynium in Asia Minor; 'Lyciae… sortes' are the oracles of Lycia, another seat of Apollo's prophecy. 'sortes' are lots, and so oracles. 'iussere' = 'iusserunt', the perfect; it serves both subjects. 'me' is understood.

sentences.t: hic amor, haec patria est.
sentences.l: this is my love, this my country.
sentences.i: that is my love, that is my homeland.
sentences.n: With 'hic amor' supply 'est'. 'hic' and 'haec' take the gender of the noun they point to ('amor', 'patria'), as Latin demonstratives regularly do. He answers her 'noster amor' (307) with a different love.

sentences.t:
Si te Karthaginis arces,
Phoenissam, Libycaeque aspectus detinet urbis,
quae tandem, Ausonia Teucros considere terra,
invidia est?
sentences.l:
If you Carthage's citadels,
a Phoenician, and the Libyan sight holds back of the city,
what, pray, Trojans in Ausonian land to settle,
grudge is it?
sentences.i: If the towers of Carthage and the sight of a Libyan city keep you here, a Phoenician, what grudge is there, pray, against the Trojans settling in the Ausonian land?
sentences.n: 'te… Phoenissam': 'Phoenissam' is in apposition to 'te', 'you, a Phoenician woman' — she too is an emigrant. 'arces… aspectus' are two subjects with a singular verb 'detinet'. 'Libycae… urbis' frames the line. 'tandem' in a question is 'pray', 'tell me'. 'Teucros considere' is an accusative and infinitive depending on 'invidia': 'grudge (that) the Trojans settle'. 'Ausonia… terra' is an ablative of place; Ausonia is an old poetic name for Italy.

sentences.t: Et nos fas extera quaerere regna.
sentences.l: We too it is right foreign to seek kingdoms.
sentences.i: We too have the right to look for a kingdom abroad.
sentences.n: With 'fas' supply 'est': 'it is right' ('fas' is divine law). 'nos' is the accusative subject of 'quaerere'. 'Et' is 'also'. 'extera… regna' frames the infinitive.

sentences.i: Me the troubled ghost of my father Anchises warns in my sleep and terrifies, every time the night covers the earth with damp shadows, every time the fiery stars come up;
sentences.n: 'Me' is the object of both 'admonet' and 'terret'. 'patris Anchisae' is a genitive that waits for its noun 'imago', the last word of the sentence. 'quotiens… quotiens' is 'whenever… whenever'. 'umentibus umbris' is an ablative of means, 'with dewy shadows'. 'astra ignea' is a subject. 'in somnis' is 'in dreams'. 'turbida' agrees with 'imago', 'troubled', 'stormy'.

sentences.t:
me puer Ascanius capitisque iniuria cari,
quem regno Hesperiae fraudo et fatalibus arvis.
sentences.l:
me the boy Ascanius and the wrong to a head dear,
whom of the kingdom of Hesperia I cheat and of the fated fields.
sentences.i: and so does the boy Ascanius, and the wrong done to one so dear, whom I am cheating of a kingdom in Hesperia and of the lands that fate has given him.
sentences.n: Supply 'admonet' with 'me puer Ascanius' (repetition of 'me', anaphora). 'capitis… cari' is an objective genitive with 'iniuria': 'the wrong done to a dear head', 'head' standing for the person. 'quem' refers to Ascanius. 'fraudo' takes an accusative of the person cheated ('quem') and an ablative of the thing he is cheated of ('regno', 'arvis'). 'Hesperiae' is a genitive: Hesperia, 'the western land', is Italy.

sentences.i: And now the gods' messenger himself, sent by Jupiter (I swear it by your head and mine), has carried the commands down through the swift air;
sentences.n: 'interpres divom' is Mercury; 'divom' is the old genitive plural (you know this '-om' ending). 'Iove missus ab ipso' — 'ipso' agrees with 'Iove'. 'testor utrumque caput' is an oath, 'I call both our heads to witness'; Greenough prints it between dashes, the second without spaces, so the unit runs on. 'celeris' = 'celeres', '-is' accusative plural, agreeing with 'auras'. 'mandata' is the object of 'detulit', the perfect of 'defero'.

sentences.t:
ipse deum manifesto in lumine vidi
intrantem muros, vocemque his auribus hausi.
sentences.l:
myself the god in clear light I saw
entering the walls, and his voice with these ears drank in.
sentences.i: I saw the god myself in the clear light of day as he came within the walls, and with these ears I drank in his voice.
sentences.n: 'deum' here is the accusative singular, 'the god', not the old genitive plural: 'intrantem', a present participle, agrees with it. 'manifesto in lumine' is 'in open light'. 'his auribus' is an ablative of means. 'hausi' is the perfect of 'haurio', 'drink in': a strong word for listening.

sentences.t: Desine meque tuis incendere teque querelis:
sentences.l: Cease both me with your and yourself to inflame complaints:
sentences.i: Stop setting both of us on fire with your complaints:
sentences.n: 'Desine' is the imperative of 'desino', 'stop', with an infinitive. 'meque… teque' is the double '-que', 'both me and you'. 'tuis… querelis' is an ablative of means, split around 'incendere teque'.

sentences.t: Italiam non sponte sequor.”
sentences.l: Italy not of my own will I follow.”
sentences.i: It is not by my own choice that I make for Italy.”
sentences.n: 'non sponte' is 'not of (my) own accord'. The line is a half-line: the Aeneid was left unfinished at Virgil's death, and Greenough prints such incomplete lines as they stand. The closing quotation mark is Greenough's: Aeneas's speech ends here.

sentences.t:
Talia dicentem iamdudum aversa tuetur,
huc illuc volvens oculos, totumque pererrat
luminibus tacitis, et sic accensa profatur:
sentences.l:
Him saying such things for a long time, turned away, she watches,
here and there rolling her eyes, and all of him she wanders over
with eyes silent, and thus inflamed speaks out:
sentences.i: While he was saying this she had been watching him all along, turned half away, rolling her eyes this way and that, travelling over the whole of him with silent looks; and then, on fire, she spoke out:
sentences.n: This line begins a new paragraph in Greenough. 'Talia dicentem' is a present participle in the accusative, agreeing with an understood 'eum', object of 'tuetur'. 'iamdudum' with a present ('tuetur') is 'has been … for a long time'. 'aversa' is a perfect participle, 'turned away'. 'huc illuc', 'hither and thither'. 'totum' is 'the whole of him'. 'luminibus tacitis' is an ablative of means. 'accensa' is the perfect participle of 'accendo', 'set on fire'. 'profatur' is the present of the deponent 'profor', 'speak out'.

sentences.t:
“Nec tibi diva parens, generis nec Dardanus auctor,
perfide; sed duris genuit te cautibus horrens
Caucasus, Hyrcanaeque admorunt ubera tigres.
sentences.l:
“Not to you a goddess parent, nor of the race Dardanus the founder,
faithless one; but on hard crags begot you bristling
Caucasus, and Hyrcanian moved udders to you, tigresses.
sentences.i: “No goddess was your mother, no Dardanus the founder of your race, you traitor: it was the Caucasus, rough with jagged rocks, that bore you, and Hyrcanian tigresses that gave you suck.
sentences.n: Dido's second speech opens here, so Greenough prints the opening quotation mark; it runs to line 387. 'tibi' is a dative of possession with 'est' (or 'fuit') understood: 'there was no goddess-mother to you'. Venus was his mother; Dardanus was the founder of the Trojan line. 'perfide' is a vocative, as at 305. 'duris… cautibus' can go with 'genuit', 'bore you on hard crags' (as the literal version keeps it), or with 'horrens', 'bristling with hard crags' (as the translation takes it). 'horrens' agrees with 'Caucasus', 'bristling'. 'admorunt' is a shortened form of 'admoverunt': 'brought (their) udders to (you)'. Hyrcania lay by the Caspian Sea. The idea goes back to Patroclus's reproach of Achilles in the Iliad (Book 16): his parents were not Peleus and Thetis but the sea and the cliffs.

sentences.t: Nam quid dissimulo, aut quae me ad maiora reservo?
sentences.l: For why do I pretend, or for what greater things do I keep myself?
sentences.i: For why should I hide my feelings, or what worse wrong am I saving myself for?
sentences.n: 'quid' is 'why'. 'dissimulo' and 'reservo' are presents used where English says 'should I'. 'quae… ad maiora' is 'for what greater (wrongs)'. She recalls her first word to him, 'Dissimulare' (305).

sentences.t: Num fletu ingemuit nostro?
sentences.l: Did he groan at weeping of ours?
sentences.i: Did he groan when I wept?
sentences.n: 'Num' asks a question expecting the answer 'no'. She now speaks of Aeneas in the third person, as if he were not standing there. 'fletu… nostro' is an ablative, 'at my weeping'; 'nostro' is the plural of the poets for 'meo'. 'ingemuit' is the perfect of 'ingemo'.

sentences.t: Num lumina flexit?
sentences.l: Did he turn his eyes?
sentences.i: Did he turn his eyes towards me?
sentences.n: 'lumina flexit' answers lines 331–332, where he 'kept his eyes unmoved' ('immota tenebat lumina'). 'flexit' is the perfect of 'flecto'.

sentences.t: Num lacrimas victus dedit, aut miseratus amantem est?
sentences.l: Did he tears, overcome, give, or pity the one loving him?
sentences.i: Was he so far overcome as to shed a tear, or did he pity the woman who loved him?
sentences.n: 'victus' is the perfect participle of 'vinco', 'overcome'. 'miseratus… est' is the perfect of the deponent 'miseror', split by its object 'amantem', a present participle used as a noun, 'the one who loves (him)'.

sentences.t: Quae quibus anteferam?
sentences.l: What before what should I put?
sentences.i: What should I say first, what after?
sentences.n: 'Quae quibus anteferam?' is literally 'which things to which shall I prefer?': there is so much to complain of that she cannot choose. 'anteferam' is most naturally a deliberative subjunctive (the form is also the future); 'quibus' is a dative with the compound verb.

sentences.t:
Iam iam nec maxuma Iuno,
nec Saturnius haec oculis pater aspicit aequis.
sentences.l:
Now, now neither greatest Juno
nor the Saturnian father these things with eyes looks at fair.
sentences.i: Now, now neither Juno the great nor the Father, son of Saturn, looks on these things with impartial eyes.
sentences.n: 'Iam iam' is emphatic, 'now at last'. 'maxuma' is Greenough's old spelling of 'maxima'. 'Saturnius… pater' is Jupiter, son of Saturn. The two subjects share a singular verb, 'aspicit'. 'oculis… aequis' is an ablative, 'with fair eyes': the gods are not just to her. Juno was the goddess of marriage, and the patron of Carthage.

sentences.t: Nusquam tuta fides.
sentences.l: Nowhere is safe faith.
sentences.i: Faith is safe nowhere.
sentences.n: Supply 'est'. 'fides' is good faith, loyalty to a promise.

sentences.t:
Eiectum litore, egentem
excepi, et regni demens in parte locavi;
sentences.l:
Cast out on the shore, destitute,
I took him in, and of my kingdom, mad, in a part placed him;
sentences.i: He was cast up on my shore, a beggar, and I took him in, and like a fool I gave him a share of my kingdom;
sentences.n: 'Eiectum' and 'egentem' agree with an understood 'eum', object of 'excepi'. 'litore' is an ablative, 'on the shore' or 'from the sea onto the shore'. 'demens' is nominative, agreeing with the subject 'I': 'mad as I was'. 'regni… in parte' frames 'demens'. 'excepi' is the perfect of 'excipio', 'take in, receive'.

sentences.t: amissam classem, socios a morte reduxi.
sentences.l: his lost fleet, his comrades from death I brought back.
sentences.i: his lost fleet, his companions, I brought back from death.
sentences.n: 'amissam' is the perfect participle of 'amitto', agreeing with 'classem'. 'reduxi' governs both 'classem' and 'socios' with no connecting word (asyndeton). The ships lost in the storm of Book I were found again at Carthage.

sentences.t: Heu furiis incensa feror!
sentences.l: Alas, by furies inflamed I am carried!
sentences.i: Ah, I am on fire with frenzy, and swept away!
sentences.n: 'furiis' is an ablative of means, 'by madness' (the furies of passion, perhaps also the Furies themselves). 'incensa' is the perfect participle of 'incendo', agreeing with the subject. 'feror' is the present passive of 'fero', 'I am carried away'.

sentences.t:
Nunc augur Apollo,
nunc Lyciae sortes, nunc et Iove missus ab ipso
interpres divom fert horrida iussa per auras.
sentences.l:
Now the augur Apollo,
now the Lycian lots, now also by Jove sent himself
the interpreter of the gods brings dreadful orders through the breezes.
sentences.i: Now it is the prophet Apollo, now the oracles of Lycia, now the gods' own messenger, sent by Jupiter himself, bringing terrible commands through the air.
sentences.n: Dido throws Aeneas's own words back at him: 'Lyciae sortes' (346), 'Iove missus ab ipso interpres divom' and 'per auras' (356–357). 'nunc… nunc… nunc' is anaphora, with a sneer in it. 'augur' is a Roman priest who read omens, here applied to Apollo. 'divom' is the old genitive plural again. 'horrida iussa' is a neuter plural, the object of 'fert'.

sentences.t:
Scilicet is Superis labor est, ea cura quietos
sollicitat.
sentences.l:
No doubt this for the Gods is a labour, this care, them at peace,
troubles.
sentences.i: No doubt the gods above take trouble over this; no doubt this is the care that disturbs their peace.
sentences.n: 'Scilicet' is sarcastic, 'of course'. 'is' takes the gender of 'labor', and 'ea' of 'cura', as at 347. 'Superis' is a dative of possession: 'this is a labour to the gods'. 'quietos' (them, the gods, 'at rest') is the object of 'sollicitat'. The idea that the gods live untroubled and care nothing for human affairs belongs to Epicurean teaching, and Dido uses it with irony.

sentences.t: Neque te teneo, neque dicta refello.
sentences.l: Neither you do I hold, nor your words refute.
sentences.i: I am not holding you, nor do I answer what you say.
sentences.n: 'Neque… neque' is 'neither… nor'. 'teneo' answers her own question 'nec te… tenet' (307–308). 'refello' is 'refute'.

sentences.t: I, sequere Italiam ventis, pete regna per undas.
sentences.l: Go, follow Italy with the winds, seek kingdoms through the waves.
sentences.i: Go, chase Italy with the winds behind you; go after your kingdom over the waves.
sentences.n: 'I' is the imperative of 'eo', 'go'. 'sequere' is the imperative of the deponent 'sequor'. 'ventis' is an ablative of means. 'pete' is the imperative of 'peto'. Three commands, bitter in their brevity.

sentences.t:
Spero equidem mediis, si quid pia numina possunt,
supplicia hausurum scopulis, et nomine Dido
saepe vocaturum.
sentences.l:
I hope indeed, in the midst, if anything holy powers can,
punishments you will drain on the rocks, and by name Dido
often will call.
sentences.i: I hope, if the righteous powers of heaven can do anything, that you will drink your punishment to the dregs out among the rocks, and call often on Dido by name.
sentences.n: 'hausurum' and 'vocaturum' are future infinitives ('esse' understood) in an accusative and infinitive after 'Spero', with 'te' understood. 'mediis… scopulis' is an ablative of place, 'in the midst of the rocks' (of a shipwreck). 'si quid' is 'if (they can do) anything'; 'quid' is an internal accusative with 'possunt'. 'pia numina' are gods who care for right. 'supplicia hausurum' is 'drain punishments', as if drinking a cup. 'Dido' is here an accusative (the name keeps the same form), object of 'vocaturum'; 'nomine', 'by name'.

sentences.t:
Sequar atris ignibus absens,
et, cum frigida mors anima seduxerit artus,
omnibus umbra locis adero.
sentences.l:
I shall follow with black fires, absent,
and, when cold death from my soul has parted my limbs,
in all places as a shade I shall be there.
sentences.i: Far off, I will follow you with black fires, and when cold death has parted my limbs from my soul, my ghost will be with you everywhere.
sentences.n: 'Sequar' is the future of the deponent 'sequor'. 'atris ignibus' is an ablative, 'with black fires', like the torches of the avenging Furies, or of her own funeral. 'absens', 'though absent'. 'seduxerit' is the future perfect: 'when death shall have parted'. 'anima' is an ablative of separation, 'from the soul'; 'artus' is the object. 'omnibus… locis' is an ablative of place with no preposition. 'umbra' is nominative in apposition to the subject, 'as a shade'. 'adero' is the future of 'adsum'.

sentences.t: Dabis, improbe, poenas.
sentences.l: You will pay, wicked one, the penalty.
sentences.i: You will pay for this, villain.
sentences.n: 'poenas dare' is the regular idiom, 'to pay the penalty'. 'improbe' is a vocative, 'shameless one'. 'Dabis' is the future.

sentences.t: Audiam et haec Manis veniet mihi fama sub imos.”
sentences.l: I shall hear, and this to the Shades will come to me, report, beneath the lowest.”
sentences.i: I shall hear of it; the news will come down to me among the deepest dead.”
sentences.n: 'Audiam' is the future. 'et' is 'and'. 'haec… fama' frames the line: 'this report'. 'Manis' = 'Manes', the '-is' accusative plural, 'the spirits of the dead'; 'sub imos Manis' is 'down to the lowest shades'. 'mihi' is a dative, 'to me'. The closing quotation mark is Greenough's: Dido's speech ends here.

sentences.t:
His medium dictis sermonem abrumpit, et auras
aegra fugit, seque ex oculis avertit et aufert,
linquens multa metu cunctantem et multa parantem
dicere.
sentences.l:
With these words, in the middle, her speech she breaks off, and the air
sick she flees, and herself from his eyes turns away and takes off,
leaving him, much from fear hesitating and much preparing
to say.
sentences.i: With these words she broke off in the middle of what she was saying and, sick at heart, fled from the light of day, turning away and taking herself from his sight, leaving him hesitating long in fear, with much that he was making ready to say.
sentences.n: 'His… dictis' is an ablative, 'with these words'. 'medium… sermonem' is split by 'dictis': 'her speech in the middle'. 'auras… fugit' is 'flees the open air'. 'aegra' agrees with the subject, 'sick at heart'. 'seque… avertit et aufert' — 'se' is the object of both verbs. 'linquens' is a present participle, agreeing with the subject; its object is an understood 'eum' (Aeneas), with whom 'cunctantem' and 'parantem' agree. 'multa… multa' is repeated: 'much… much'. 'metu' is an ablative of cause. 'dicere' depends on 'parantem' and is held over to the next line.

sentences.t:
Suscipiunt famulae, conlapsaque membra
marmoreo referunt thalamo stratisque reponunt.
sentences.l:
Take her up her maids, and her collapsed limbs
to the marble chamber they carry back and on coverlets lay down.
sentences.i: Her maids caught her up, and carried her fainting body back to her marble chamber, and laid it on the cushions.
sentences.n: 'Suscipiunt' is 'they catch her up' from below. 'conlapsa' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'conlabor', agreeing with 'membra', 'limbs that had fallen'. 'marmoreo… thalamo' has no preposition: poetry often uses a plain case for the place to which, here 'to the marble chamber'. 'stratis' is 'on the coverlets'; 'strata' is a neuter plural noun from 'sterno', 'spread'. 'reponunt' is 'lay back'.

sentences.t:
At pius Aeneas, quamquam lenire dolentem
solando cupit et dictis avertere curas,
multa gemens magnoque animum labefactus amore,
iussa tamen divom exsequitur, classemque revisit.
sentences.l:
But dutiful Aeneas, although to soothe her grieving
by consoling he desires and with words to turn away her cares,
much groaning and in his mind shaken by great love,
the orders nevertheless of the gods carries out, and revisits his fleet.
sentences.i: But Aeneas, true to his duty, though he longs to ease her grief with comfort and turn her pain aside with words, and groans deeply, his heart shaken by his great love, still carries out the gods' commands and goes back to his fleet.
sentences.n: This line begins a new paragraph in Greenough. 'pius' is Aeneas's standing epithet, set here with care: his loyalty to the gods is what costs Dido. 'quamquam' takes the indicative ('cupit'). 'dolentem' is a present participle used as a noun, 'her grieving' (Dido). 'solando' is the ablative of the gerund of 'solor', 'by consoling'. 'multa' is an internal accusative with 'gemens', 'groaning much'. 'animum' is an accusative of respect with the passive participle 'labefactus', 'shaken in mind'; 'magno… amore' is an ablative of cause. 'divom' is the old genitive plural again. 'exsequitur' is the present of the deponent 'exsequor'. 'tamen' marks the turn.

sentences.t:
Tum vero Teucri incumbunt, et litore celsas
deducunt toto naves: natat uncta carina;
sentences.l:
Then indeed the Trojans set to, and on the shore the lofty
they launch, along the whole, ships: floats the greased keel;
sentences.i: Then the Trojans fell to work in earnest, and all along the shore launched their tall ships: the tarred hulls float;
sentences.n: 'Tum vero' marks a vivid moment, 'then truly'. 'Teucri' is the Trojans, from Teucer, an early king of Troy. 'incumbunt' is 'lean into (the work)'. 'litore… toto' is an ablative of place, and 'celsas… naves' is split across the line-end. 'deducunt' is the regular word for hauling ships down into the sea. 'carina', 'keel', stands for the ship (synecdoche) and the singular for the whole fleet. 'uncta' is the perfect participle of 'unguo', 'smeared' with pitch.

sentences.t:
frondentisque ferunt remos et robora silvis
infabricata, fugae studio.
sentences.l:
and leafy they bring oars and timbers from the woods
unworked, from eagerness for flight.
sentences.i: they bring oars still in leaf and unshaped timber from the woods, in their eagerness to be gone.
sentences.n: 'frondentis' = 'frondentes', the '-is' accusative plural, agreeing with 'remos': oars made from branches so freshly cut that the leaves are still on them. 'robora' is 'oak timbers'. 'silvis' is an ablative, 'from the woods'. 'infabricata' agrees with 'robora', 'unwrought', and is held over to the next line. 'fugae studio' is an ablative of cause. Line 400 is another half-line, one of the poem's unfinished verses.

sentences.t: Migrantis cernas, totaque ex urbe ruentis.
sentences.l: Moving out you could see them, and from the whole city rushing.
sentences.i: You could see them moving out, pouring from every part of the city.
sentences.n: 'cernas' is a potential subjunctive, 'you could see', addressed to the reader. 'Migrantis… ruentis' = 'migrantes… ruentes', present participles in the '-is' accusative plural, with 'eos' (the Trojans) understood. 'tota ex urbe' puts the preposition between adjective and noun.

sentences.t:
Ac velut ingentem formicae farris acervum
cum populant, hiemis memores, tectoque reponunt;
sentences.l:
And as when a huge of spelt the ants heap
plunder, of winter mindful, and in their home store it;
sentences.i: As when ants are plundering a great heap of grain, mindful of the winter, and storing it away in their home;
sentences.n: A simile begins: 'velut… cum' is 'just as when'. 'ingentem… acervum' frames the line around 'formicae farris'. 'farris' is the genitive of 'far', spelt, a kind of wheat. 'populant' is 'lay waste, plunder', an active form of a verb more often deponent ('populor'). 'hiemis memores' — 'memor' takes the genitive. 'tecto' is 'in (their) home', the plain case for the place to which. The Trojans on the shore, seen from a height, look like an army of ants.

sentences.t:
it nigrum campis agmen, praedamque per herbas
convectant calle angusto;
sentences.l:
goes the black over the plains column, and the plunder through the grass
they carry together along a path narrow;
sentences.i: the black column moves over the fields, and they carry their booty together along a narrow track through the grass;
sentences.n: 'it' is the present of 'eo', 'goes'. 'nigrum… agmen' frames 'campis', an ablative of place. 'agmen' is a military word, 'column on the march'; the simile keeps the language of war ('praedam', 'agmina cogunt'). 'convectant' is a frequentative, 'keep carrying together'. 'calle angusto' is an ablative of the route, 'by a narrow path'.

sentences.t:
pars grandia trudunt
obnixae frumenta umeris;
sentences.l:
part great push
straining the grains with their shoulders;
sentences.i: some heave great grains forward, straining with their shoulders;
sentences.n: 'pars… trudunt' — a collective singular 'pars' with a plural verb, a construction by sense. 'obnixae' is feminine plural, agreeing with the ants ('formicae') understood in 'pars'; it is the perfect participle of 'obnitor', used of Aeneas at 332. 'grandia… frumenta' frames the phrase: 'large grains'. 'umeris' is an ablative of means.

sentences.t:
pars agmina cogunt
castigantque moras;
sentences.l:
part the columns gather
and chastise delays;
sentences.i: some keep the columns closed up and punish stragglers;
sentences.n: 'agmina cogunt' is the military phrase for bringing up the rear and keeping a column together. 'castigant moras' is 'rebuke delays': the laggards are hurried along. The plural verbs again go with the sense of 'pars'.

sentences.t: opere omnis semita fervet.
sentences.l: with work all the path seethes.
sentences.i: the whole track is seething with work.
sentences.n: 'opere' is an ablative of cause, 'with the work'. 'omnis semita' is 'the whole path'. 'fervet' is 'boils, seethes', a vivid close to the simile and the part.
